items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that the singular values of a real matrix [MATH: A] are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix [MATH: A^T \! A.]

Content:
Also, since [MATH: A^T \! A] is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of [MATH: A^T \! A] must be always non-negative real numbers.

Content:
Let's compute the singular values of the matrix [MATH: A,] given by

Content:
[MATH: [0|2; − 2|0; 2|1]]

Content:
Now, since

Content:
- [MATH: A] is a [MATH: 3 \times 2] matrix, and
- [MATH: A^T] is a [MATH: 2 \times 3] matrix,

Content:
then [MATH: A^T \! A] must be a [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix:

Content:
[MATH: \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} =
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}]

Content:
Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate [MATH: A^T \! A\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: A^{T}A|= [0|2; − 2|0; 2|1]^{T}[0|2; − 2|0; 2|1]; = [0|− 2|2; 2|0|1][0|2; − 2|0; 2|1]; = [8|2; 2|5]]

Content:
Next, we compute the eigenvalues of [MATH: A^T \! A\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: |A^{T}A − λI||= 0;|8 − λ|2; 2|5 − λ||= 0; (8 − λ)(5 − λ) − 4|= 0; λ^{2} − 13λ + 36|= 0; (λ − 9)(λ − 4)|= 0; λ|= 9, 4]

Content:
Therefore, the singular values of [MATH: A] are as follows:

Content:
[MATH: σ_{1}|= sqrt(λ_{1}) = sqrt(9) = 3; σ_{2}|= sqrt(λ_{2}) = sqrt(4) = 2]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.
- If [MATH: A] is a [MATH: m\times n] matrix, then [MATH: A^T A] is a [MATH: n\times n] positive semi-definite matrix. This means that [MATH: A] has at most [MATH: n] distinct singular values.

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following statements are true?

  1. Any [MATH: 1\times4] matrix [MATH: A] has at most [MATH: 1] singular value.

  2. Any [MATH: 4\times2] matrix [MATH: A] has at most [MATH: 2] distinct singular values.

  3. The matrix [MATH: [− 1|0; 0|1]] has one negative singular value.
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following statements are true?

1. Any [MATH: 1\times4] matrix [MATH: A] has at most [MATH: 1] singular value.
2. Any [MATH: 4\times2] matrix [MATH: A] has at most [MATH: 2] distinct singular values.
3. The matrix [MATH: [− 1|0; 0|1]] has one negative singular value.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The singular values of the matrix [MATH: A] are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix [MATH: A^T \! A.]

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is false. Since [MATH: A] is a [MATH: 1 \times 4] matrix and [MATH: A^T] is a [MATH: 4\times 1] matrix, [MATH: A^T \! A] must be a [MATH: 4 \times 4] matrix: [MATH: \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times {\large 1}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 1} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A} = \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A^T \! A}] Hence, [MATH: A] has at most [MATH: 4] distinct singular values.

  • Statement II is true. Since [MATH: A] is a [MATH: 4 \times 2] matrix and [MATH: A^T] is a [MATH: 2\times 4] matrix, [MATH: A^T \! A] must be a [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix: [MATH: \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 4}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}] Hence, [MATH: A] has at most [MATH: 2] distinct singular values.

  • Statement III is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, [MATH: A] cannot have a negative singular value.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The singular values of the matrix [MATH: A] are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix [MATH: A^T \! A.]

First, we calculate [MATH: A^T \! A\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: A^{T}A|= [1|2; 2|1]^{T}[1|2; 2|1]; = [1|2; 2|1][1|2; 2|1]; = [5|4; 4|5]]

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of [MATH: A^T \! A\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: |A^{T}A − λI||= 0;|5 − λ|4; 4|5 − λ||= 0; (5 − λ)^{2} − 16|= 0; λ^{2} − 10λ + 9|= 0; (λ − 1)(λ − 9)|= 0; λ|= 9, 1]

Therefore, the singular values of [MATH: A] are as follows:

[MATH: σ_{1}|= sqrt(λ_{1}) = sqrt(9) = 3; σ_{2}|= sqrt(λ_{2}) = sqrt(1) = 1]
